name: AI for Patient Recruitment and Matching
title: AI for Patient Recruitment and Matching
answer: Recruitment is the most common reason trials run late, and AI matching of patient records to eligibility criteria is one of the clearest wins. In one published example an AI system screened 1,053 patients in about 2 hours against roughly 150 hours by hand.

reading.body:
Recruitment is the most common reason trials run late, and AI matching of patient records to eligibility criteria is one of the clearest wins. In one published example an AI system screened 1,053 patients in about 2 hours against roughly 150 hours by hand.

The pattern is a screening step that was bound by human reading time. A review in PMC reported an AI driven matching system in China screened 1,053 patients 98.7 percent faster than manual review. The constraint that moved was not the availability of patient records but the labor to read them against eligibility criteria.

For AI specifically, this is a case where the model does not need to be right about medicine, only fast and consistent about matching text to criteria. That makes it one of the few clinical AI uses where the value shows up as hours rather than as a new capability. The data does not say whether the matched patients were ultimately enrolled, consented, or representative of the trial population.

Matching only helps if sites can act on it. Pair AI screening with site capacity to contact and consent patients. A 2026 review in a Nature portfolio journal compared AI recruitment platforms and their measured impact on enrollment, which suggests the field is still measuring whether faster screening converts into completed trials. Nothing here covers cost, regulatory acceptance, or whether the 98.7 percent figure generalizes beyond the single system described.

explainer:
Finding patients who meet a trial's eligibility criteria is slow because the criteria are detailed and the information is scattered through health records, much of it in free text such as clinic notes and pathology reports. Coordinators often screen records by hand, and many trials miss enrolment targets or close sites for lack of patients.

AI matching uses natural language processing to read records and compare each patient against the criteria, producing a ranked list of likely candidates for staff to review. Published systems report dramatic cuts in screening time. Matching alone does not enrol patients, though: someone still has to contact them, explain the trial and obtain consent, and patients must be willing and able to take part. AI also brings a fairness question, since patients whose records are thinner or less standardised may be missed, which can worsen under-representation in trials.

Why recruitment is the bottleneck

Most trials miss their enrolment timelines, and many sites enrol few or no patients. Finding eligible patients means searching records for people who meet dozens of criteria, which has been manual work by study coordinators, and it means reaching patients who may never hear about a trial. Slow recruitment is the single largest cause of delayed trials, which is why matching is one of the most funded uses of AI in clinical development.

How AI matching works

Models read eligibility criteria and electronic health records, including unstructured notes, and identify patients who appear to qualify, ranked by how well they match. Hospital systems run this against their own patients to alert clinicians; sponsors and vendors run it across networks of sites to choose where to open a trial; and patient facing services use it to suggest trials to people who search. Reported results include large reductions in screening time per patient and more patients identified at sites that already had them in their records.

What has to be handled carefully

Matching uses identifiable health data, so it runs under privacy rules that differ by country and usually inside the institution that holds the records. Models trained on past trial populations can reproduce their under representation of some groups, so sponsors check who the model surfaces against the population with the disease. The final eligibility decision is clinical and stays with the investigator, since a model reading notes can miss an exclusion that a clinician would catch. And patients still have to be approached and consent, which no model does for them.
